# SciRate Daily Digest — 2026-09-16

## 1. Exact efficient simulation of noisy logical magic states using Clifford stabilizers

[arXiv:2609.16929](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16929) · [SciRate](https://scirate.com/arxiv/2609.16929)

*Yugo Takada, Stephen D. Bartlett, Dominic J. Williamson*

**TL;DR** The paper shows that many logical magic states (|T̄⟩, |C̄C̄Z̄⟩, |H̄⟩) are the unique +1 eigenstate of a group generated by Pauli stabilizers *plus* non-Pauli Clifford operators ("Clifford stabilizers"), and that this group can be updated under circuit-level Pauli noise using rules directly analogous to the Gottesman–Knill tableau updates. This yields an exact, polynomial-time simulator for a broad class of noisy magic-state preparation protocols implementing third-level Clifford-hierarchy gates, demonstrated by exact simulation of magic state cultivation up to fault distance 7 — previously out of reach.

**The big picture** Estimating how well a fault-tolerant computer can prepare the exotic resource states needed for universal quantum computing currently forces a bad choice: exact simulation that blows up exponentially, or replacing the protocol with a cheaper stand-in whose performance is only assumed to be representative. This work observes that these resource states, while not ordinary stabilizer states, are still pinned down uniquely by a group of symmetry operators drawn from the easy-to-simulate gate set, and that noise merely dresses those symmetries in a controlled way. Exploiting this, a noisy non-Clifford preparation circuit can be replaced by an exactly equivalent easy circuit, so benchmarking becomes as cheap as ordinary error-correction simulation. Protocol designers can now measure, rather than guess, the fidelity of the very protocols slated for early useful fault tolerance.

**Key contributions**
- Formal notion of a (possibly non-Abelian) Clifford-stabilizer group whose generators *effectively* commute on the stabilizer subspace, with group-commutator bookkeeping.
- Proof that circuit-level Pauli noise — including hook errors that propagate as *Clifford* (S, S†, CZ) errors onto data qubits — only produces Pauli-Z "dressings," guaranteeing every protocol measurement effectively commutes or anticommutes with every tracked generator, at all times.
- Generalized update rules (pivot multiplication, random-sign replacement) plus a proposition that deterministic outcomes remain readable off the tracked generators under a stated algebraic condition.
- A reduction mapping each sampled noisy non-Clifford circuit to a *single* Clifford circuit reproducing the exact outcome distribution — no stabilizer/Pauli-rank decomposition, hence no dependence on that rank.
- Extension beyond stabilizer measurements: injection circuits, transversal non-Clifford gates, code growth, midcircuit measurement with correction, ancilla resets.
- Validation against state-vector simulation at f=3 (10⁸ samples) and exact cultivation results at f=5, 7.

**How it works** Errors conjugate transversal or fold-transversal Pauli/Clifford factors into Pauli-dressed versions; since dressings are Z-type up to phase and commute with the diagonal Clifford factors, iterated commutators truncate and residual commutators are always Z-type stabilizers (known up to a tracked sign). Current generators are products of at most a few dressed originals, so commutation reduces to a product of ±I factors, permitting tableau-style updates and, ultimately, an equivalent Pauli-stabilizer/Clifford circuit constructed in polynomial preprocessing.

**Why it matters** Cultivation and related low-overhead protocols have been benchmarked using S|+⟩ proxies with no guarantee of fidelity to the T-state target; this removes that caveat and scales to regimes relevant for useful FTQC.

**Caveats** Requires "admissible" Clifford-stabilizer structure (CSS-like Pauli sectors, transversal/fold-transversal generators, commuting Clifford factors in the diagonal treatment, a primary-support-exactness condition for deterministic outcomes) and third-level-hierarchy targets. Pauli noise only — no coherent or amplitude-damping errors. At f=7 the per-shot cost is fine but plain Monte Carlo cannot resolve the very low logical error rate; importance-sampling integration is left open.

## 2. Quantum Compiler Design for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing

[arXiv:2609.17465](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17465) · [SciRate](https://scirate.com/arxiv/2609.17465)

*Chenghong Zhu, Jiahan Chen, Keming He, Hongshun Yao, Zhaohui Yang, Jin-Guo Liu, Anbang Wu, Xiaotong Ni et al.*

**TL;DR** A full-stack survey of compilation for fault-tolerant quantum computing, organizing the literature into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC compilation (lattice surgery, code surgery for qLDPC codes, magic-state and code-switching resource management), physical-level realization on superconducting/trapped-ion/neutral-atom hardware, and decoder-runtime integration (detector error models, real-time decoders, Pauli/Clifford frames, window decoding). It argues that QEC-aware compilation is qualitatively different from NISQ mapping/routing, because correctness now requires preserving circuit-level distance, fault-propagation structure, and the detector information the decoder needs — not just unitary equivalence. An accompanying maintained paper list is provided.

**The big picture** Error-corrected quantum computers do not execute gates on bare qubits; every logical operation is a protocol built from encoded blocks, repeated error-checking measurements, and classical feedback that must complete fast enough to keep up with the machine. This means the software that translates an algorithm into hardware instructions can no longer be a circuit optimizer that minimizes gate count and depth: it must choose fault-tolerant protocols, allocate encoded data and scratch space, schedule everything under hardware movement and timing limits, and hand a measurement stream to a real-time classical decoder. The survey maps the scattered work on these problems onto a single stack and shows where the layers are still poorly connected. This matters because the practical cost of error correction is now set as much by compilation and decoding choices as by the code itself.

**Key contributions**
- A three-layer taxonomy (logical compilation / physical realization / decoder runtime) tying together communities that publish separately (quantum information, computer architecture, PL/compilers, EDA).
- Systematic review of surface-code lattice-surgery compilers (solver-based, heuristic, resource-aware) and of the more heterogeneous beyond-surface-code landscape: transversal/fold-transversal gates, code-surgery gadgets, bridges and adapters for qLDPC blocks.
- Coverage of non-Clifford resource coordination: magic-state distillation scheduling, code/gauge switching, and early-FT models based on injected rotations.
- Platform-specific physical-layer treatment: coupling-graph and crosstalk constraints (superconducting), shuttling/zone management in QCCD (trapped ion), movement legality and blockade/addressing (neutral atom).
- An explicit open-problems agenda: cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compiler abstractions, compiler–decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, benchmark standardization.
- Quantitative evidence of field growth: QEC papers at ISCA/ASPLOS/HPCA/MICRO rising from sparse 2021 acceptances to substantially higher 2025 counts, with rising acceptance ratios.

**How it works** The framing is driven by theory constraints (Eastin–Knill, Bravyi–König locality bounds, the Bravyi–Poulin–Terhal trade-off with distance-squared scaling) that force universality to combine complementary mechanisms, which in turn define distinct compiler problems. For surface codes, merge/split primitives are recast as an instruction set with explicit space-time cost: patch placement fixes which joint Pauli measurements are local, routing fixes ancilla area, scheduling fixes parallelism. For high-rate codes such as bivariate bicycle families (e.g., the [[144,12,12]] "gross" code with depth-7 syndrome circuits and two-layer planar layouts), no single patch abstraction exists, so the compiler must reason about per-code logical addressing and inter-block interactions. The runtime layer is treated as part of the compilation target, since syndrome-extraction schedules determine the detector error model.

**Why it matters** With below-threshold memories, real-time decoding demonstrations, and end-to-end qLDPC processor blueprints now published, the bottleneck is shifting to the software stack. Useful entry point for architects and compiler researchers moving from NISQ mapping to FTQC, and a checklist for anyone designing an integrated stack.

**Caveats** It is a taxonomy and literature map, not an evaluation: no head-to-head quantitative comparison of compilers on common benchmarks — indeed the absence of such benchmarks is listed as an open problem. Scope excludes photonic/fusion-based and spin-qubit platforms, and excludes code-construction, threshold-analysis, and decoder-theory work except where it constrains compilation, so readers seeking those angles need other references. Coverage includes preprints, so some surveyed methods are unvalidated.

## 3. Hyperbolic color codes with constant rate and polynomial distance

[arXiv:2609.16125](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16125) · [SciRate](https://scirate.com/arxiv/2609.16125)

*Shun Hasegawa, Hayata Yamasaki*

**TL;DR** The authors construct the first hyperbolic color codes that simultaneously achieve constant encoding rate and polynomial distance, in every dimension $D\ge 4$. For $D=2m$, the type-$m$ color code on Guth–Lubotzky-style arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds gives $[[n,\Theta(n),\Omega(n^{(m-1)/(m(2m+1))})]]$ — e.g. rate-$\Theta(1)$ and $d=\Omega(n^{1/10})$ in four dimensions — and they tabulate explicit $k$- and $d$-exponents for all $D\ge4$, $2\le i\le D-2$.

**The big picture** Color codes are a favorite playground for fault tolerance: they support rich transversal gate sets, single-shot error correction, and self-correction arguments. But until now, color codes built on negatively curved geometries topped out at logarithmic distance, so they could not offer the exponential error suppression one wants from a high-rate code. This work shows that the geometric constructions known to give good high-dimensional toric codes on hyperbolic manifolds can be converted into color codes without losing either the constant rate or the polynomially growing distance, and it supplies explicit growth exponents for every dimension and code type. That makes color-code-specific fault-tolerance protocols available in the constant-overhead regime.

**Key contributions**
- Proof that the barycentric subdivision of *any* triangulation of a closed $D$-manifold is a colex (satisfying the recursive colorable-ball definition), giving a general recipe for color codes on arbitrary manifolds — avoiding the dual-complex ambiguity of the cell-inflation approach.
- A rigorous proof that the known color-to-toric restriction morphism yields a *lower bound* on the color-code distance: $d^Z_{CC_i}\ge\max_{c^*}\min_C d^Z_{TC_i(X_{C\sqcup\{c^*\}})}$, with the $X$-sector bounded by type-$(D-i)$ restricted toric codes.
- A systolic distance bound for toric codes on *restricted lattices* (not the original triangulation), via a lemma that nontrivial cycles of $X_C$ remain nontrivial in $X$.
- Explicit exponents: Betti-number growth from Xue's bounds (polynomial $k$ for $2\le i\le D-2$) plus Lück approximation to get *linear* growth of $b_{D/2}$ in even $D$ (hence constant rate for both the color and toric codes); systolic exponents from Kim's bound, extended from prime to arbitrary congruence ideals.

**How it works** Fix a torsion-free congruence subgroup $\Gamma_{N_0}\subset SO_f(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2])$ for $f=-\sqrt2 x_0^2+\sum x_i^2$, triangulate the base manifold $M_0$, barycentrically subdivide to get a colex $X_0$, then pull back along the covering tower $M_N=\Gamma_N\backslash\mathbb{H}^D$. Number of logicals is $\binom{D}{i}b_i$; distance is bounded below by the restricted-lattice toric distances, which are bounded below by $c_1\cdot\mathrm{sys}_j(M_N,g)$ since each simplex has bounded volume under the local isometry.

**Why it matters** Relevant to anyone pursuing constant-space-overhead fault tolerance on reconfigurable hardware (neutral atoms, ion shuttling) where geometric locality is relaxed, and to those studying single-shot decoding or transversal non-Clifford gates, which are natural in the color-code setting.

**Caveats** The distance exponents are small ($1/10$ in $D=4$) and are lower bounds only; no matching upper bounds or numerics. Stabilizer weights grow with $D$ (barycentric subdivision inflates the complex substantially), and no concrete qubit counts, decoders, thresholds, or explicit logical-gate constructions are given — the promised color-code protocol advantages remain prospective. Constants depend on the unspecified base manifold and triangulation, and the constant-rate case requires even $D$ and type $D/2$.

## 4. Environmental records unlock universal quantum computation from thermal decoherence

[arXiv:2609.16460](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16460) · [SciRate](https://scirate.com/arxiv/2609.16460)

*Chenfeng Cao, Qi Zhao*

**TL;DR** For a stabilizer (Clifford + Pauli measurement + feedforward) processor whose only noise sits in monitored thermal idles under independent local Markovian baths, the authors prove an exact computational dichotomy at $(1-p_e)T_2/T_1=1$: if every idle location sits at or below this line, all record branches admit nonnegative stabilizer decompositions and the whole adaptive circuit *plus* its time-resolved jump record is efficiently classically sampleable; if a single reusable location sits above it, postselecting the no-jump branch of a $|+\rangle$ idle heralds distillable magic and gives BQP-universality with overhead polynomial in $1/\chi$, where $\chi=(1-p_e)T_2/T_1-1$. Crucially, the same physical exposure can be simulable or universal depending only on which one bit of the environmental record the controller keeps.

**The big picture** Decoherence is normally thought of as something that destroys quantum computational power. Here the authors show that if a processor's only quantum resource is the information the environment happens to write down about energy exchanges, then merely knowing that nothing was emitted or absorbed during an idle period can act as a magic-state factory — turning an otherwise classically simulable Clifford machine into a fully universal quantum computer. The dividing line is set entirely by standard device calibration numbers (relaxation time, coherence time, thermal population), and current superconducting hardware sits right at it within calibration uncertainty. The punchline is that which environmental records a controller retains, not just how noisy the hardware is, belongs in the specification of a quantum processor.

**Key contributions**
- Exact boundary $\chi=0$ and matching two-sided classification theorem (simulable side; universal side with a single repeatedly accessible location, so the criterion is $\chi_{\max}$).
- Nonnegative decomposition of the no-jump channel into identity, complete dephasing, and $|0\rangle$-projection, valid branchwise on entangled inputs and under adaptive reuse.
- A continuous-time uniformized tableau sampler: state-independent total proposal rate $1/T_2^{(i)}$ per exposed rail, giving exact sampling of outputs *and* records at cost polynomial in total exposure $H_{\max}$ in local-$T_2$ units, with a finite-precision guarantee.
- Stabilizer measure-and-prepare threshold $t_{\rm mp}$ for the record-averaged channel ($e^{-t/T_2}=p_e(1-e^{-t/T_1})$), with a necessary-and-sufficient five-setting product-stabilizer witness; this kills magic on *arbitrary many-qubit* inputs, strictly stronger than one-qubit magic breaking.
- Proof that the exchange bit and terminal $ZZ$ parity are information-theoretically incomparable at $p_e>0$: margins $\gamma_{\rm q}\ge\gamma_{\rm par}\ge\gamma_{\varnothing}$, with a fixed-exposure window where $\gamma_{\rm q}>0\ge\gamma_{\rm par}$ (a thermal round trip restores parity after coherence is already gone). A randomized acceptance rule interpolates with threshold $r_c=\gamma_{\rm q}/(\gamma_{\rm q}-\gamma_{\rm par})$.
- Detector-loss analysis: with terminal parity, only $M=m_\uparrow m_\downarrow$ enters and only at second order, so the $\chi=0$ boundary survives any inefficiency; at $p_e=1/4,T_2=2T_1,t_H$ one needs $M<0.548$ (≈26% efficiency per direction). Without parity, missed absorption shifts the line as $p_e\to(1+m_\uparrow)p_e$.
- Correlated-bath counterexample: two qubits in a reciprocal common bath open a short-time margin $|\kappa|t/T_1$ in the single-excitation code space for any $\kappa\neq0$, even when all local $\chi_i\le0$ — locality of the criterion is an artifact of bath factorization.

**How it works** In the energy-jump unraveling, detected jumps are $Z$ measurements plus resets (stabilizer), so all nonclassicality is in the quiet branch $\mathcal N_t$. Its three exponents order as $\Gamma_\uparrow\le\Gamma_\downarrow\le1/T_2$ exactly when $p_e\le1/2$ and $\chi\le0$, which is precisely nonnegativity. Above the boundary coherence outlives excited-state survival weight, pushing the accepted $|+\rangle$ output across a stabilizer-octahedron facet by $\gamma_{\rm q}=e^{-t/T_2}-e^{-\Gamma_\downarrow t}$, optimized at $t_{\rm q}^\star=T_2\ln(1+\chi)/\chi$ with $\gamma_{\rm q}^\star=\chi(1+\chi)^{-1-1/\chi}\to\chi/e$ and success probability $>1/e$; an $\{I,H\}$ twirl lands it in Reichardt's Steane-code distillation region, needing $O(\log 1/\chi)$ rounds. A branch-criterion lemma ($\gamma_\ell=c_\ell-\min\{A_\ell,D_\ell\}$) shows the one-use stabilizer-assisted yield is $[\gamma_\ell]_+$ and that coarse-graining can only lose yield, so the exchange bit already saturates the full record's yield.

**Why it matters** Erasure-conversion and quantum-jump-monitoring architectures already expose exactly these event flags; the paper says such flags can herald injection states above the boundary and should be treated as a computational resource, not just decoder data. Quoted transmon numbers give $\chi\approx0.45$ (Ramsey $T_2$) and $\chi\approx0.007\pm0.015$ (echo $T_2$), i.e. the boundary is inside current calibration uncertainty. Relevant to fault-tolerance architects, magic-state resource theorists, and continuous-measurement experimentalists.

**Caveats** Stabilizer control is assumed noiseless (ideal-Clifford/noisy-ancilla abstraction), so this is not a hardware proposal. The criterion uses *homogeneous* $T_2$ with quasistatic broadening excluded; the sign of $\chi$ on real devices depends on whether Ramsey or echo times are the right proxy, and $\chi>0$ requires $T_1/(1-p_e)<T_2\le2T_1$, a narrow window. Results apply only to unsplit, time-homogeneous energy-counting idles with known energy axes; diffusive records, continuous feedback, intermediate parity checks, and other unravelings are unclassified, as are general correlated baths (no $\chi_{\max}$ analogue). Realizing the instrument requires the correct measurement backaction, not merely a flag. Overhead is set by the vanishing margin near threshold, and postselection on exponentially rare records remains inefficient.

## 5. Evaluating Verified Autonomy in Quantum Engineering

[arXiv:2609.17439](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17439) · [SciRate](https://scirate.com/arxiv/2609.17439)

*Naixu Guo, Changhao Li, Siyu Cheng, Qicheng Tang, Binzhao Luo, Bikun Li, Yuxuan Du, Shihao Ru et al.*

**TL;DR** Quantum-Harbor is a sandboxed virtual quantum laboratory in which LLM agents must plan experiments, call instrument-like tools, and submit results that a hidden grader either recomputes from a private evidence log or re-tests on fresh simulated data. On QIQCBench — 49 expert-authored, cross-layer quantum engineering tasks — 17 frontier agentic systems span pass rates from 78% down to 3%, with the dominant failure mode (937 of 1,510 failures) being running out of the 3-hour budget without ever submitting an answer.

**The big picture** Building and running quantum hardware still depends on expert judgment: deciding which measurement to take next, noticing when a stale calibration no longer applies, and knowing when enough evidence has been gathered. If AI agents are to take over parts of this work, we need to know not just whether they output the right number, but whether that number is actually supported by measurements they took. This work builds a controlled fake laboratory where every instrument call is logged and hidden from the agent, so claims can be audited or re-tested on fresh data, and then uses it to show that today's best agents are capable but highly unreliable at complete laboratory workflows.

**Key contributions**
- Quantum-Harbor: a two-container (agent / hidden sidecar) environment built on Harbor, exposing lab tools over MCP, with interchangeable simulator, replay, and live-hardware backends behind platform abstractions ("qtypes") for transmons, ions, neutral atoms, photonics.
- *Evidence-bound grading*: numerical claims are recomputed from the private log of executed jobs; calibrations/designs are replayed against fresh draws from hidden noise parameters — closing the "report a number you never measured" loophole.
- QIQCBench: 49 tasks over 36 qtypes, six categories, mapped onto five stack layers; 39 pass/fail, 7 "racing" tasks scored by a ridge-regularized Bradley–Terry Elo fit, 3 infrastructure canaries.
- A first systematic measurement of *verified autonomy*, with a failure taxonomy (no-submission / science failure / contract failure).

**How it works** Tasks are end-to-end mini-projects with an intended solution path plus "honest traps" drawn from real labs — e.g., a 114-qubit transmon lattice-surgery task where the notebook recommends reusing a decoder calibrated on separate patches, but merging introduces seam-correlated errors invisible in that data; the best run reached 6.65×10⁻⁴/cycle distance-5 memory error and 0.131 mean logical-CNOT error on fresh syndromes. A second flagship task requires surrogate modeling of a hidden 60-qubit circuit with 6 free parameters, predicting 1,770 two-qubit correlations on 40 held-out inputs. Racing trials are compared pairwise, with gate-passing trials always beating gate-failing ones.

**Why it matters** The benchmark discriminates strongly among systems that cluster tightly on general agentic benchmarks (eight of the 17 sit within 54–62% on AutomationBench-AA; six within 31 Elo on GDPval). Failures look like poor experimental judgment — stale priors, budget mismanagement, discarding in-hand results — not missing physics knowledge, pointing at harness design as the near-term lever. Relevant to anyone building lab-automation agents or agentic science evals.

**Caveats** Everything ran on simulators; live-hardware backends are supported but untested here. Only 3 trials/task (Wilson intervals do not cover task-selection uncertainty); success is intermittent (only 34% of 249 passing system–task pairs pass all three attempts). Two tasks were unsolved by every system, and results conflate model capability with harness (Codex vs. Claude Code vs. OpenCode). Agents had internet access, and hidden thresholds are unpublished — reproducibility and contamination control depend on the maintainers.
